analysis.one_liner: Requires FDA review of food ingredients companies currently declare safe on their own.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in December 2023, referred to the Senate health committee, and never received a vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current rules, a company can decide on its own that a new food ingredient is 'generally recognized as safe' (GRAS) and put it in food without telling the FDA. This bill would end that self-certification: companies would have to submit safety data to the FDA, wait out a public review period, and prove their ingredients don't cause cancer or reproductive harm. It would also create a new FDA office required to re-examine the safety of chemicals already in the food supply on an ongoing basis. The bill was introduced by Senator Markey with three Democratic cosponsors, referred to the Senate HELP Committee, and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, especially infants, children, pregnant women, and other vulnerable groups the bill names: chemicals in food would face independent federal safety review before reaching grocery shelves, with safety data made public and chemicals already in food periodically re-examined.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Food consumers, especially children and pregnant women

how_it_helps.text: Ends the current practice letting food manufacturers decide for themselves that an ingredient is 'generally recognized as safe' and market it without FDA sign-off.

Bars substances the National Toxicology Program has identified as causing cancer or reproductive/developmental harm from being designated GRAS, with extra safety margins for vulnerable groups like infants and pregnant women.

Creates an FDA office that must publicly reassess the safety of at least 10 food substances or classes every three years, and requires manufacturers' GRAS determinations and supporting data to be posted publicly for a 90-day review period.

analysis.who_pays: Food and ingredient manufacturers, which would lose the ability to self-certify ingredients as safe and would bear the cost of safety testing, FDA submissions, and possible reformulation of products using chemicals found unsafe.

drawbacks.text: Requiring FDA review of every new GRAS determination would slow food innovation and add regulatory costs for food manufacturers, especially small companies introducing new ingredients.
The mandatory reassessment cycle (at least 10 substances or classes every three years) would be a demanding new workload for FDA, and the bill does not specify new funding for the Office it creates.
The rulemaking deadlines (proposed revision within one year) are ambitious for an agency with a slow rulemaking record.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health benefit—closing a loophole that lets companies self-certify food chemicals as safe without FDA sign-off—is substantial and the bill posed no direct cost to consumers; the real cost is regulatory burden and reformulation expense for food manufacturers, plus slower introduction of new ingredients. Given the size of the American food supply and documented concerns about chemicals in food, the tradeoff weighed heavily toward the public. The bill's fatal weakness was political: it had no Republican support and went nowhere.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read once in the Senate and sent to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which took no action on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Markey introduced the bill on December 4, 2023, with Senators Booker, Blumenthal, and Warren as original cosponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
No further action was recorded — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill never attracted a cosponsor from outside its small Democratic group.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food and chemical manufacturers are better off: the GRAS self-certification system that lets companies add ingredients without independent federal review remains untouched.

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to end self-certification of food ingredient safety and create a new FDA food chemical safety office.

for.name: Sens. Booker, Blumenthal, and Warren
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no other senators joined.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Senate leadership and the HELP Committee majority
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration or floor time, leaving it to die at adjournment.

sides.party_line_note: All four supporters were Democrats and the bill attracted no Republican cosponsors; it also never advanced past referral in the Democratic-controlled Senate.

industries.note: The bill ends self-affirmed GRAS marketing and requires FDA review, public posting of safety data, and periodic reassessment of chemicals already in food. Consumers get stronger safety screening at no direct cost to them; the industry bears compliance costs and could lose the use of some chemicals.

industries.industry: Food chemical testing and toxicology consultants
industries.note: Companies that run GRAS panels and safety assessments would face stricter conflict-of-interest rules, but the mandatory reassessment cycle could increase demand for safety evaluations.
